title: C++: lifetimes, abstractions, and concurrency
description: Study C++20 ownership, object lifetime, generic code, memory ordering, and performance through explicit invariants and local experiments.

lessons.title: Storage is not an object lifetime
lessons.summary: Distinguish allocated storage from a live object
objectives: Distinguish allocated storage from a live object.
Track the lifetime of references and views.
lessons.body:
## Core idea

Storage is a region of bytes; an object has a lifetime governed by construction and destruction rules. A pointer can still contain an address after the object at that address has died. Non-owning views and references do not extend arbitrary owners. Whenever a C++ function hands you a reference or view, ask one question: who owns the data, and can it die before I finish reading?

## Worked example

A view into a local string dangles at function return. A view into a caller-owned string can remain valid only while that string exists and operations do not invalidate the referenced character storage.

## Try it

Classify returns of a local value, a reference to a local, a view into a parameter, and a view into static storage. Write the required caller contract for each valid case.

## Check your work

Returning a value is ordinarily safe because it transfers or constructs an owned result. Explain validity by lifetime and invalidation rules, not by whether the old bytes still happen to be visible.

## Primary reading

- [C++ Core Guidelines](https://isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines/CppCoreGuidelines)

lessons.title: RAII and exception-safe resource ownership
objectives: Make cleanup follow object lifetime.
State the exception guarantee of a multi-step operation.
lessons.body:
## Core idea

RAII ties resource release to an owning object destructor. Files, locks, memory, and sockets all benefit from a single owner with deterministic cleanup. A basic exception guarantee preserves valid invariants; a strong guarantee leaves observable state unchanged on failure. Destructors should normally avoid throwing. Smart pointers express ownership, while raw pointers can still be useful non-owning observers. Go decides when memory is freed with its garbage collector, later; C++ decides now, in the destructor, deterministically.

## Worked example

Acquire a resource into a unique_ptr or a dedicated handle wrapper before performing later operations that might fail. If a later constructor throws, already-constructed members are destroyed. A bare resource acquired before that ownership transfer may leak.

### Follow the steps

Imagine this constructor sequence for a Session object. A member opens a file into a unique handle. A second member allocates a buffer. The constructor body then validates the input and throws. Fully constructed members unwind in reverse declaration order: buffer first, file handle second. The Session destructor itself does not run because the Session never finished construction.

Move the throw into the buffer's construction. The file handle is still destroyed, but the buffer member never completed construction. Draw both traces and add a logging handle in a small local test. The log should show exactly one release for every successful acquisition.

## Try it

Design a movable file-handle wrapper with a clear invalid state. Then sketch replacing a configuration by constructing a candidate first and committing only after validation.

## Check your work

Every successful acquisition has one owner and one release path. Move transfers ownership, moved-from destruction is safe, and failure does not leave a half-updated configuration.

## Primary reading

Optional reading after the example and exercise.

- [C++ Core Guidelines, R.1](https://isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines/CppCoreGuidelines#Rr-raii) · Read the rule on resource handles for the acquisition and cleanup pattern used here.

lessons.title: Value semantics and moved-from objects
lessons.summary: Explain copying versus moving without assuming a move is free
objectives: Explain copying versus moving without assuming a move is free.
Use the rule of zero for ordinary resource-containing types.
lessons.body:
## Core idea

A copy creates another value according to its type contract. A move permits transferring resources from an expiring object, but the actual operation is type-defined. std::move is a cast that enables move overload resolution; it does not itself move bytes. If every member cleans up after itself (std::string, std::unique_ptr), you usually do not need to hand-write destructor, copy or move. A moved-from standard library object remains valid but its exact value is generally unspecified unless documented.

## Worked example

A struct holding a string and vector can usually rely on their constructors and destructors. Adding a manual destructor unnecessarily can change implicit move generation and create surprising performance or correctness consequences.

## Try it

Trace a vector of records through copy construction, move construction, and destruction. Identify why storing a borrowed pointer inside the record changes the ownership story.

## Check your work

Do not read a specific old string value after moving from it. Explain which operations remain valid and why using std::move on a const value may still select a copy.

## Primary reading

- [C++ Core Guidelines](https://isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines/CppCoreGuidelines)

lessons.title: A view outlives its owner
lessons.body:
## The problem to understand

A function returns a `std::string_view` into a local string. What is the strongest correct statement about the caller’s read? Assume C++20. The fact that this example might print the expected bytes on your machine is not a guarantee.

```cpp
std::string_view label() {
    std::string text = "market-data";
    return text;
}
auto v = label();
std::cout << v;
```

## The mental model

The local string is destroyed at function exit, so the returned view does not designate a live character sequence. Reading through it has undefined behavior. `std::string_view` is a non-owning pointer-and-length abstraction; it does not extend the owner’s lifetime.

Return `std::string` to transfer an owned result, or return a view only into storage with a documented lifetime that exceeds every use. Small-string optimization does not rescue the local object’s lifetime; it can simply change where the invalid storage was located.

## Check your understanding

- Identify string_view as non-owning.
- Locate destruction of the local string.
- Choose an owned result or a valid external lifetime.

## Think one step further

Is returning a view into a string parameter safe when the caller passes a temporary?

## Primary reading

- [cppreference · std::string_view](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/string/basic_string_view.html) · Check which operations invalidate the view and how small strings store characters.
objectives: Identify string_view as non-owning.
Locate destruction of the local string.

lessons.title: Container choice follows invalidation and access
lessons.summary: Select containers using access and invalidation requirements
objectives: Select containers using access and invalidation requirements.
Separate capacity from the number of live elements.
lessons.body:
## Core idea

A vector provides contiguous elements and cheap indexed access; growth can relocate them. Linked structures avoid some relocation but add allocation, pointer chasing, and different invalidation rules. Reserve changes vector capacity, not its size, so it does not construct elements. Standard algorithms express transformations independently of a particular container, but their iterator and ordering requirements still matter.

An unordered_map rehashes when the load factor exceeds its limit. Rehashing invalidates iterators but preserves references and pointers to existing elements. Do not iterate while inserting: an insertion can trigger a rehash and break your loop's iterator. Erasing a single element keeps every other element's references valid.

Braced initialization also rejects narrowing conversions: `int x{3.7}` is ill-formed, while `int x = 3.7` compiles and silently truncates. Prefer braces when you want that rejection.

## Worked example

Reserving space for 100 records does not make records[50] a valid element when size is zero. Appending constructs elements. Retaining pointers across append is valid only under the relevant documented invalidation conditions.

### Follow the steps

Start with a vector whose size and capacity are both three. Save an iterator to its second element, then append a fourth element. Growth requires reallocation, which invalidates that iterator. The element is still at index one if you only appended, but the old address may no longer denote it.

Run the thought experiment again after reserving capacity for four before taking the iterator. Appending one element leaves existing element iterators valid, while the old past-the-end iterator is invalidated. Finally erase the first element and explain why index one now denotes a different record. Use stable record IDs if callers need identity across erasure.

## Try it

Choose a representation for records appended in bursts and scanned repeatedly. Document how callers obtain stable identifiers even if the vector relocates.

## Check your work

Indices or external IDs survive some changes that raw element pointers do not, but erasure and reordering need their own policy. Justify a linked list only using measured or required behavior.

## Primary reading

Optional reading after the example and exercise.

- [C++ working draft, vector modifiers](https://eel.is/c++draft/vector.modifiers) · Check the rules for insertions and erasure, including past-the-end iterator invalidation.

lessons.title: Templates, concepts, and runtime polymorphism
lessons.summary: Express generic requirements with C++20 concepts
objectives: Express generic requirements with C++20 concepts.
Choose dynamic dispatch when runtime heterogeneity is required.
lessons.body:
## Core idea

Templates generate code for types meeting their requirements. Concepts make syntactic constraints visible, but a concept checks your comparator is callable, not that it behaves; a comparator whose answer changes between calls still compiles and still corrupts the sort. Virtual interfaces support runtime substitution and heterogeneous ownership. If deletion through a base pointer is allowed, that destruction contract must be safe. Dispatch and ownership are separate design decisions.

A lambda captures by value, copying each variable at creation, or by reference, aliasing the original. A by-reference capture can outlive the referenced variable; a callback invoked after the function returns reads freed storage. For callbacks that outlive the call, copy by value or capture a shared_ptr to share ownership. Go escapes such variables to the heap; C++ makes the lifetime a capture decision.

## Worked example

A generic sorting helper may require a comparator, yet a comparator that changes its answer over time still breaks the algorithm contract. A virtual sink registry can select concrete destinations at runtime without templating every caller.

## Try it

Sketch a constrained record encoder and a polymorphic output sink. List semantic requirements that cannot be enforced by a concept alone.

## Check your work

Explain which decisions occur at compile time and runtime. Include object destruction, error propagation, and comparator or encoding determinism in the contract.

## Primary reading

- [C++ Core Guidelines](https://isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines/CppCoreGuidelines)

objectives: Identify deletion through Base* as the problematic operation.
Explain the limitation of unique_ptr’s default deleter.

lessons.title: The iterator that survived until it did not
lessons.body:
## The problem to understand

Repair this loop so that every original even element is duplicated exactly once at the end of the vector. The implementation must be correct for any initial capacity. Explain why reserving more capacity is not, by itself, a complete repair for a range-for loop.

```cpp
std::vector<int> v = {1, 2, 3, 4};
for (const auto& x : v) {
    if (x % 2 == 0) v.push_back(x);
}
```

## The mental model

Record the original size, iterate by index only up to that size, and copy the current value before any push: `const auto n = v.size(); for (size_t i=0; i<n; ++i) { auto x=v[i]; if(x%2==0) v.push_back(x); }`. No reference or iterator is retained across a potential reallocation, and newly appended elements are excluded.

Reallocation invalidates all element iterators and references. Even without reallocation, push_back invalidates the old past-the-end iterator. A range-for typically captures both begin and end before iteration, so making capacity large enough does not preserve that cached end iterator. A two-pass collection into a second vector is also valid.

## Check your understanding

- Restrict traversal to the original size.
- Avoid retaining a reference across push_back.
- Explain both reallocation and past-the-end invalidation.

## Think one step further

What exception-safety guarantee does the repaired function offer if an allocation fails halfway through?

## Primary reading

- [cppreference · std::vector](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/vector.html) · Check the iterator and reference invalidation notes for push_back and reallocation.
objectives: Restrict traversal to the original size.
Avoid retaining a reference across push_back.

lessons.title: Data races and happens-before
lessons.summary: Separate atomicity from visibility of other memory
objectives: Separate atomicity from visibility of other memory.
Build a happens-before argument for publication.
lessons.body:
## Core idea

If two threads touch the same ordinary variable and at least one writes, with nothing ordering them, the program is broken; an atomic is what creates that ordering. An atomic flag protects its own access; additional memory-order relationships are needed to publish ordinary payload data. Mutex unlock and later successful lock provide a standard synchronization mechanism. Release/acquire creates an ordering only when the acquire load actually reads the value the release store wrote.

A condition_variable can return from wait without a matching notify; that is a spurious wakeup. `wait(lock, pred)` rechecks pred before every wait, so write a check-then-wait loop and never trust a bare wait. The same loop also absorbs a notify that fired before the consumer reached the wait. Go's sync.Cond documents the same loop.

## Worked example

A producer fills a payload then release-stores ready. A consumer that acquire-loads that publication can read the payload under a valid one-shot lifetime protocol. Replacing both operations with relaxed does not provide that publication edge.

### Follow the steps

Use one producer and one consumer with a payload initially unshared. Draw four events: producer writes payload; producer stores true with release; consumer loads true with acquire from that store; consumer reads payload. The local ordering on each thread plus the synchronizes-with edge across the flag orders the payload write before the read.

Replace both flag operations with relaxed operations. The flag remains atomic, but the cross-thread ordering for the ordinary payload disappears. For a reusable mailbox, add a second transfer of ownership before the producer can overwrite the slot. Label which access protects the new transfer.

## Try it

Draw an event graph for a one-shot mailbox. Add every write, flag operation, read, and object destruction. Then consider a producer trying to reuse the mailbox immediately.

## Check your work

The one-shot proof includes initialization and lifetime. Reuse requires a return ownership edge or another protocol; observing ready once does not make indefinite concurrent mutation safe.

## Primary reading

Optional reading after the example and exercise.

- [C++ working draft, Data races](https://eel.is/c++draft/intro.races) · Read the definitions of synchronizes-with and happens-before.

lessons.title: Use tools to challenge a correctness claim
lessons.summary: Match sanitizers to likely defect classes
objectives: Match sanitizers to likely defect classes.
Keep performance experiments separate from instrumented diagnostics.
lessons.body:
## Core idea

Address and undefined-behavior sanitizers can expose many invalid accesses and operations; thread sanitizers target executed data races. Their coverage is useful but incomplete. A sanitizer-clean run is evidence about tested executions, not a proof that every lifetime or synchronization contract holds. Instrumentation also changes execution costs, so performance results need an appropriate uninstrumented build.

## Worked example

An iterator invalidation bug may pass a small test because capacity never grows. Force reallocation and test erasure boundaries. A thread test should exercise shutdown and contention rather than only a single successful operation.

## Try it

Create a local validation matrix for a queue: boundary tests, address/undefined checks, race checks where supported, and a release benchmark. State a distinct purpose for each.

## Check your work

Record compiler, standard mode, options, and workload. Do not compare sanitizer runtime to a release result as though the difference measured an algorithm improvement.

## Primary reading

- [C++ Core Guidelines](https://isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines/CppCoreGuidelines)

lessons.title: The flag that protects nothing else
lessons.body:
## The problem to understand

A producer writes an ordinary payload, then sets `ready`. A consumer spins until ready is true and reads the payload. There is one producer, one consumer, one publication, and the payload remains alive. Explain why the shown relaxed protocol is invalid, and provide the minimum straightforward ordering repair. Describe exactly which load must observe which store.

```cpp
// producer
payload = 42;
ready.store(true, std::memory_order_relaxed);

// consumer
while (!ready.load(std::memory_order_relaxed)) {}
use(payload);
```

## The mental model

Atomicity of the flag does not establish ordering for the non-atomic payload. With relaxed operations there is no synchronizes-with edge between the threads, so the conflicting payload accesses are not ordered by happens-before and the program has a data race.

Use a release store to ready after initialization and an acquire load in the successful consumer check. When that acquire reads the value from the release store, initialization happens before the payload read. The failed polling loads need not themselves establish publication. This proof assumes the payload is not concurrently overwritten and remains alive. Seq_cst also works, but adds an ordering requirement that the one-shot protocol does not need.

## Check your understanding

- Separate the atomic flag from the non-atomic payload accesses.
- Use a release store and an acquire observation of it.
- State the one-shot, lifetime, and no-overwrite assumptions.

## Think one step further

Can the consumer safely reset ready with Relaxed and let the producer overwrite payload?

## Primary reading

- [C++ working draft · data races](https://eel.is/c++draft/intro.races)
objectives: Separate the atomic flag from the non-atomic payload accesses.
Use a release store and an acquire observation of it.

lessons.title: Correct atomics, terrible scaling
lessons.body:
## The problem to understand

Two threads repeatedly increment two different `std::atomic<uint64_t>` counters located next to each other. Throughput drops when the threads run on different cores. Assume the counters share a coherence line. Which interventions or claims are valid? Select all that apply.

## The mental model

Independent atomic variables can still share a coherence line. Each core’s write requires ownership of that line, creating coherence traffic even though the program has no data race. Separating the hot counters onto distinct target-appropriate cache lines can reduce that traffic. Thread-local accumulation with occasional aggregation can reduce it further when delayed visibility is acceptable.

Relaxed ordering may reduce ordering constraints but does not eliminate the need for exclusive line ownership on writes. A fixed padding size is a platform assumption, not a universal property. Measure on the intended hardware and consider object alignment and array layout as well as field spacing.

## Check your understanding

- Distinguish false sharing from a data race.
- Recognize padding/alignment and local aggregation as possible repairs.
- Explain why Relaxed alone does not remove coherence ownership traffic.

## Think one step further

Why might padding every object make an entirely different workload slower?

## Primary reading

- [cppreference · hardware_destructive_interference_size](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/thread/hardware_destructive_interference_size.html) · Check what the constant represents and its platform-dependent value.
objectives: Distinguish false sharing from a data race.
Recognize padding/alignment and local aggregation as possible repairs.

lessons.title: Data layout and allocation budgets
lessons.summary: Relate layout to locality without sacrificing lifetime correctness
objectives: Relate layout to locality without sacrificing lifetime correctness.
Account for allocation and alignment in a hot path.
lessons.body:
## Core idea

Contiguous scans can exploit locality and prefetching, while pointer-rich graphs may serialize cache misses. Separating hot fields from cold metadata can reduce bytes touched per operation. Alignment can prevent some false sharing, but padding also increases footprint. A hand-rolled pool buys speed at the cost of who-frees-what puzzles; write the ownership rule down first, measure second, build third.

## Worked example

A scan that uses only price and quantity pays unnecessary bandwidth if every record also embeds a large text field. Keeping cold text elsewhere can reduce traffic, provided the associated identifiers remain valid.

## Try it

Compare an array-of-structs and a split hot/cold layout for a scan workload. Predict bytes read per record and include construction and teardown costs in a separate measurement.

## Check your work

Both implementations return identical results. Report whether the bottleneck is bandwidth, latency, or compute, and do not assume a smaller object automatically produces a faster complete application.

## Primary reading

- [C++ Core Guidelines](https://isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines/CppCoreGuidelines)

lessons.title: Review a low-level API before optimizing it
lessons.summary: Write ownership and failure contracts at an API boundary
objectives: Write ownership and failure contracts at an API boundary.
Identify whether callers can violate an internal invariant.
lessons.body:
## Core idea

A low-level component needs a precise contract for ownership transfer, thread topology, invalidation, errors, and shutdown. If a caller can destroy an endpoint while another thread uses it, a fast internal algorithm is irrelevant. Design the API so the wrong thing cannot be written down; a try_push that returns false without taking the value beats one where callers guess who owns the event. Keep lock-free progress claims separate from memory safety and application latency claims.

A shared_ptr keeps its object alive while any owner exists, so an API can hand out references without a separate lifetime contract. A cycle of shared_ptr never frees; the counts never reach zero. A weak_ptr observes without owning; it breaks the cycle, and its lock() yields a shared_ptr only while some owner remains. Go's garbage collector reclaims cycles; reference counting does not.

## Worked example

A try_push operation returning false must specify whether it consumed the input. A queue destructor must state whether producers have already stopped and what happens to queued values.

## Try it

Write a one-page API contract for a bounded queue of move-only values. Include full, empty, throwing construction, endpoint destruction, and concurrent shutdown.

## Check your work

A reviewer can tell who owns a value after every outcome. Each progress claim has stated assumptions and destruction occurs only after active users are synchronized.

## Primary reading

- [C++ Core Guidelines](https://isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines/CppCoreGuidelines)

lessons.title: Removing a node is the easy part
lessons.body:
## The problem to understand

A lock-free stack uses an atomic head pointer. A popper reads head and its next pointer, then performs compare_exchange. Another thread can remove and free the first node during that interval. Explain both the use-after-free and ABA hazards. Compare hazard pointers and epoch-based reclamation, including what happens when a participating thread stalls.

## The mental model

A successful pointer CAS only validates the head value at that instant; it does not prove that a node dereferenced earlier remained alive. A node can be freed before its next field is read. Allocator reuse can also restore the same address, making a pointer-only CAS miss intervening changes: ABA.

Hazard pointers publish protected nodes, then require readers to revalidate the source pointer before dereferencing. Removed nodes are retired and reclaimed only when no hazard protects them. A stalled thread can pin its protected nodes. Epoch reclamation waits until every reader has checked in at a point where it holds no node; so one paused reader can block cleanup forever, and retired nodes can pile up without bound. Tagged pointers mitigate some ABA cases but do not alone make dereferencing freed memory safe. Include shutdown, registration, memory bounds, and allocator behavior in the design. A seqlock couples an atomic version counter with payload reads and retries when the version changed, and the recheck is valid only if the payload loads are themselves atomic, because a plain racing read is undefined behavior that a later comparison cannot undo.

## Check your understanding

- Show how dereference can race with reclamation before CAS.
- Distinguish ABA from object-lifetime safety.
- Describe hazard publication plus revalidation and epoch quiescence.
- Compare stalled-reader retention and operational complexity.

## Think one step further

What progress guarantee does the full stack offer once its allocator and reclamation mechanism are included?

## Primary reading

- [cppreference · std::atomic](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/atomic/atomic.html) · Check the atomic operations a lock-free stack and a seqlock version counter rely on.
objectives: Show how dereference can race with reclamation before CAS.
Distinguish ABA from object-lifetime safety.

lessons.title: Capstone: a bounded event processor in C++20
lessons.summary: Integrate RAII, containers, synchronization, and measurement
objectives: Integrate RAII, containers, synchronization, and measurement.
Validate a component across failure and shutdown.
lessons.body:
## Core idea

Build a bounded producer-consumer event processor with move-only events and explicit overload behavior. Start with a mutex-based implementation, then optimize only if a profile identifies a meaningful limit. Define the order of accepted events, who owns rejected values, how handlers fail, and how shutdown drains or discards pending work.

If handlers aggregate floating-point measurements, the order of a parallel sum changes the low-order bits; fix a reduction order or a tolerance when results must be reproducible.

## Worked example

If a handler throws, RAII must still release its lock and event resources. A shutdown request arriving during a full queue must not require a blocked producer to complete before the consumer is allowed to drain.

### Starter exercise

Sketch a capacity-one queue of move-only events. Specify that a full try_push returns failure without taking ownership, that pop transfers the stored event, and that close prevents further pushes while allowing queued events to drain. A starter interface can expose try_push(Event&&), try_pop(), and close(), with a mutex around the queue state.

Test the contract before measuring throughput. Push event 7, try event 8 while full, verify the caller still owns 8, then pop 7. Repeat with a handler that throws and verify that the event is destroyed once and the next event can still be processed under your stated failure policy.

## Try it

Deliver implementation, ownership diagram, and tests for capacity one, full and empty transitions, handler failure, and repeated startup/shutdown. Run available sanitizers locally and compare throughput plus tail latency for two capacities.

## Check your work

Accept only with exact accounting for accepted, processed, rejected, and discarded events; safe destruction; and a documented thread contract. Explain any optimization against the safe baseline rather than assuming lock-free means faster.

## Primary reading

Optional reading after the example and exercise.

- [C++ Core Guidelines, CP.42](https://isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines/CppCoreGuidelines#Rconc-wait) · Read the condition-variable predicate rule if your queue uses a blocking wait.

prerequisites: Read basic C-style syntax, functions, and structs.
Understand pointers and compile a small program locally.
outcomes: Distinguish ownership, storage, and object lifetime in C++20.
Use RAII, value semantics, and standard containers to design safe interfaces.
Reason about synchronization and concurrent reclamation.
Validate a bounded component with tests, sanitizers, and reproducible measurements.
